CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should announce retaliatory tariffs on the remaining ~$75 billion of U.S. imports not yet covered, targeting politically sensitive sectors (agriculture, energy, autos) to maximize leverage in negotiations. Simultaneously, signal willingness to return to the negotiating table if the U.S. rolls back its May escalation, but do not make unilateral concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high and escalating. As of early August 2019, the U.S. has raised tariffs from 10% to 25% on $200 billion of Chinese goods (effective May 10, 2019), and President Trump has threatened to impose tariffs on essentially all remaining imports (~$300 billion more). The Reuters timeline shows a clear pattern of escalation: each round of U.S. tariffs has been met with Chinese retaliation, but the U.S. has far more tariff headroom remaining. The USC analysis notes that the trade war threatens China's access to U.S. markets and technology in critical future industries (AI, cloud computing, robotics, green tech), which are central to Made in China 2025. Fox Business reporting confirms that U.S. officials (Lighthizer, Mnuchin) were demanding changes to Chinese national security and trade laws — structural reforms that would undermine the CCP's industrial policy model. The threat_score of +0.55 reflects that while China's economy is under real pressure from tariffs on $250B+ of exports, China retains retaliatory tools and the domestic political capacity to absorb short-term pain through nationalist mobilization. The action_score of -1.0 (maximal retaliation) is justified because: (1) the U.S. has escalated unilaterally by raising tariffs to 25% after China reportedly backtracked on a draft deal, so retaliation is a proportionate and domestically necessary response; (2) as Sen. Graham stated, the U.S. strategy is to 'break the stranglehold China has on the supply chain' — this is an existential framing that demands a firm response; (3) White House adviser Kudlow acknowledged 'both sides will suffer,' indicating the U.S. is willing to accept pain, so concessions now would be read as weakness; (4) retaliation targeting farm-belt and energy states creates domestic political pressure on Trump ahead of the 2020 election cycle, potentially forcing a more balanced negotiation. China should retaliate firmly but leave the door open to talks, as the economic costs to both sides create mutual incentive for eventual de-escalation.
key_factors: US raised tariffs to 25% on $200B of Chinese goods (May 2019); threatened tariffs on remaining ~$300B
China backtracked on draft trade pact per Reuters, triggering US escalation
US demands structural reforms to Chinese laws (IP, market access, forced tech transfer) per USC and Fox Business reporting
White House adviser Kudlow acknowledged 'both sides will suffer' from tariffs
Sen. Graham framed US goal as breaking China's supply chain dominance
China has already retaliated on $110B of US goods; retaliation on remaining goods is available tool
Trade war threatens China's tech ambitions in AI, cloud, robotics per USC analysis
Domestic political pressure in US farm belt creates leverage for China's retaliation
